newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon's Eternit plans to up capital to wipe debt.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon's Eternit plans to up capital to wipe debt.

text.p: Lebanon's debt-plagued industrial pipemaker Eternit reported a 33 percent fall in turnover in 1996 to $12,095,000 and a loss for the year of 106 million Lebanese pounds ($68,000).
Turnover dropped to $12,095,000 from $17,966,000, partly due to fluctuations on the Syrian market, shareholders who attended Eternit's June 25 annual assembly said.
Last year was Eternit's first year on the reopened Beirut Stock Exchange which resumed trading in January 1996 after a shutdown of nearly 13 years.
Shareholders said the company reported year-end short-term debts of 23 billion pounds and long-term debts of 2.4 billion and planned to convert part of the debt into capital.
"Shareholders agreed to revalue the company's assets and call an extraordinary assembly to inject some $10 million fresh cash into capital before yearend," a shareholder said.
"The company must convert part of its debt into capital as this debt is wiping out its profits," he told Reuters.
Another shareholder said the company planned to seek new investors for the capital increase.

He said Eternit was experiencing difficulties due to a 1992 decision to set up two new production lines, partly to boost production and partly because of fears that Eternit's classical asbestos cement line at Chekaa, in north Lebanon, might be shut down for ecological reasons.
"It was essential to invest in the two new production lines for strategic reasons. Now we are well-positioned to meet future market challenges," the shareholder said.
However, another shareholder said the new production lines had been very heavy on Eternit's balance sheet because they were financed from its own resources.

Of the $9 million cost, $3 million was obtained through a long-term loan from the International Finance Corporation and $6 million was taken from working capital because of a lack of long-term facilities from banks.

"The problem is that Eternit used all their working capital for long-term investment but they had no other options at the time," a shareholder said. "A capital injection now would drastically reduce the financial overhead.

"The management wants to up capital by $10 million, which would leave some eight billion pounds uncovered, mainly those that do not carry any interest, such as advances and payments due to suppliers," he said.
Eternit's shares have performed poorly since January 1996 falling from $3.375 to $1.5 between January and November 1996. They now range between $1.5 and $2 but are frequently untraded.
They last traded on June 26 at $1.78125 on turnover of 150 shares.

"Investors don't want to buy into a company that is not making good profits. Eternit is making profits but if it is spending them on servicing debts then this is no good for investors," a financier who asked not to be identified, said.
Some financiers say Eternit might be a good long-term investment if it wins large markets with its new production lines.
"Negotiations are underway to export to the Iraqi market which was the largest export market for Eternit in pre-Gulf War days," a financier said.
"Eternit is a long-term buy. If they manage to go back to the Iraqi market, they could perform very well," he said.
$1 = 1,539.75 on Monday
